--- title: "Matrix completion and recommendation systems" subtitle: "AIDAMS -- S7" author: "Guillaume Lecué" institute: | ![](Logo-essec.jpg){width=200px} engine: knitr # execute: # eval: false format: revealjs: theme: serif slide-number: c/t width: 1600 height: 900 margin: 0.08 scrollable: true transition: fade auto-stretch: false css: custom.css knitr: opts_chunk: dev: "svg" fig.ext: "svg" engine.opts: template: "tikz-template.tex" dvisvgm.opts: - "-n" - "--libgs=/opt/homebrew/lib/libgs.dylib" --- # Introduction ## Reconstructing a matrix from few linear measurements {.smaller} :::{.box-red style="font-size: 1.15em;"} Unknown matrix $A^*\in\R^{u\times v}$, observed through $m$ linear measurements $$y_i=\inr{A^*,X_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,\qquad\text{where }\inr{A,B}=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}.$$ ::: - $uv$ unknowns parameters but only $m\ll uv$ equations: a **highly underdetermined** problem, as in compressed sensing. - It becomes solvable when the [true dimension]{.red} of $A^*$ is much smaller than $uv$, and in particular smaller than $m$. - The natural structure here is **low rank**: ${\rm rank}(A^*)=r\ll u\wedge v$. . . . ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: low rank is the low-dimensional structure of the 'signal'$A^*$" icon=false} To reconstruct a matrix from a small number of linear measurements, the low-rank assumption plays the role that sparsity played for vectors. ::: ## The rank of a matrix {.smaller} ::: {.box-blue} The [rank]{.red} of a matrix $A\in\R^{u\times v}$ is the number of non-zero singular values of $A$, i.e. the number of non-zero entries in the spectrum of $A$. ::: It is also the number of linearly independent rows or columns of $A$, i.e. the dimension of the row space or column space of $A$, which is the same as the dimension of the image of $A$. :::{.box-green} What are the rank of the following matrices? - the identity matrix $I\in\R^{u\times u}$? The matrix full of zeros? - the diagonal matrix $D={\rm diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_s, 0, \ldots, 0)$? - $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{pmatrix}$? - the $u\times v$ matrix with all entries equal to $1$? - The block matrix $B=\begin{pmatrix}A & 0 \\ 0 & A\end{pmatrix}$, where $A$ is a $u\times v$ matrix full of ones? - the matrix $A= x x^\top$, where $x\in\R^u$ is a vector? ::: ## Recommender systems by completion of the users/items matrix {.smaller} - The **users/items matrix** has entry $(i,j)$ equal to the rating of user $i$ for item $j$ when it exists, and is empty otherwise. - A **matrix completion** algorithm fills in the empty entries. - On each row (that is, for each user), recommend the items with the highest predicted ratings. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="44%"} ![](images/users_items_matrix.png){width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width="12%"}


$$\Longrightarrow$$
[Matrix completion]{style="color:#b22222"}
::: ::: {.column width="44%"} ![](images/users_items_matrix_completed.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: After matrix completion, we recommend: 1. *item 14* to *user 6*, 2. *item 16* to *user 4*, etc. ## The Netflix Prize {.spread-out} - The matrix-completion viewpoint became very popular after the **Netflix Prize**. - $480\,189$ users and $17\,770$ items (movies). - Ratings range from $1$ ("did not like it") to $5$ ("liked it very much"). - Only $100\,480\,507$ ratings were observed, about $1.2\%$ of all possible entries. . . . ::: {.box-green} **Idea:** One can build a recommender system by completing the users/items matrix. ::: . . . ::: {.box-yellow} - **Q1:** Write the data in the Netflix Prize as a matrix $A^*\in\R^{u\times v}$ and a set of linear measurements $y_i=\inr{A^*,X_i}$ (what are the $X_i$'s, $u,v$ and $m$?). - **Q2:** Imagine that you have a matrix completion algorithm that can complete the matrix $A^*$ from the linear measurements $y_i$. How would you use this algorithm to build a recommender system? ::: ## Matrix completion as linear measurements {.spread-out} - Let $E_{p,q}$ be the matrix with a $1$ at entry $(p,q)$ and $0$ elsewhere: $(E_{p,q})_{p,q}$ is the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^{u\times v}$. - If user $p$ rated item $q$ with grade $y_{p,q}$, then [$y_{p,q}=A^*_{p,q}=\inr{A^*,E_{p,q}}.$]{.blue} - With $\Omega=\{(p,q):\text{user }p\text{ rated item }q\}$, we observe $(A^*_{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\Omega}$. . . . - Completing the matrix is therefore reconstructing $A^*$ from $m=|\Omega|$ linear measurements, with $X_i\in\{E_{p,q}:1\leq p\leq u,\ 1\leq q\leq v\}$. . . . :::{.box-green} The solution set $\{A:\inr{A,X_i}=y_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}$ is an **affine space**, so without extra structure the problem has no unique solution. **Q.:** Why is the low-rank assumption a natural assumption for the users/items matrix in the Netflix Prize? ::: ## The low-rank assumption {.smaller .spread-out} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - Users fall into a small number of **profiles**: fans of science fiction, of crime films, of adventure films, and so on. - Movies fall into a small number of **themes**. - Homogeneous groups give (more or less) the same ratings to movies of the same category. - So $A^*$ is close to a **block matrix**, whose rank is of the order of the number of groups. - We assume $A^*$ is exactly low rank. The approximately low-rank and noisy cases need no new ideas. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A block-constant users/items matrix with 3 user groups and 3 item groups has rank at most 3.](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/block-matrix-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: exploit the low rank structure of the users/items matrix" icon=false} The users/items matrix is approximately low rank. Completion algorithms, and hence recommender systems, are designed to exploit this property. ::: # Convex Relaxation in Matrix Completion ## Notation and dictionary vector/matrix {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} - Inner product on $\R^{u\times v}$: $\inr{A,B}=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. - **Spectrum** $\sigma_A=(\sigma_j(A))_{j=1}^{u\wedge v}$: the singular values (square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$), with $\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{u\wedge v}(A)\geq0$. - **Schatten norms:** $\norm{A}_{S_p}=\norm{\sigma_A}_{\ell_p}=\Big(\sum_j\sigma_j(A)^p\Big)^{1/p}$, $p\geq1$. - **Rank** = number of nonzero singular values: [${\rm rank}(A)=\norm{\sigma_A}_{\ell_0}$]{.blue}. . . . | Norm | Name | Vector analog | |:---:|:---:|:---:| | $\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}$ | nuclear norm (trace norm) | $\ell_1$ | | $\norm{\cdot}_{S_2}$ | Frobenius norm (Hilbert norm of $\inr{\cdot,\cdot}$) | $\ell_2$ | | $\norm{\cdot}_{S_\infty}$ | operator norm $\sup_{\norm{x}_2=1}\norm{Ax}_2$ | $\ell_\infty$ | : {tbl-colwidths="[25, 50, 25]"} . . . - **Duality:** $\norm{A}_{S_q}=\sup\big(\inr{A,B}:\norm{B}_{S_p}\leq1\big)$ when $p^{-1}+q^{-1}=1$. - $\cS^p$: symmetric matrices; $\cS^p_+$: positive semidefinite ($A\succeq0$); $\cS^p_{++}$: positive definite ($A\succ0$); $\cO(p)=\{A:A^\top A=AA^\top=I_p\}$: orthogonal matrices. ## Rank minimization procedure :::{.box-blue style="font-size: 0.85em;"} **Problems:** Given $y_i=\inr{A^*,X_i}$ with $A^*$ of low rank: - How can $A^*$ be reconstructed exactly? - How many measurements $m$ are needed, and how should $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be chosen? - For matrix completion: what happens when the $X_i$'s must be taken in $\{E_{p,q}\}$? ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (rank minimization)" icon=false style="font-size: 0.75em;"} $$\min\Big({\rm rank}(A):\inr{A,X_i}=y_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\Big)$$ ::: . . . ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} - The analog of $\ell_0$ minimization (the rank is the $\ell_0$ norm of the spectrum): look for the solution of smallest rank among all matrices with the same measurements. - We could study it as we studied $\ell_0$ minimization, but it fails for the **same algorithmic reason**. ::: ## Rank minimization is NP-hard {.smaller .spread-out} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Finding a solution to rank minimization over an affine space, $\min_{\cA(A)=y}{\rm rank}(A)$, is NP-hard in general. ::: . . . 1. **Reduction from $\ell_0$.** Start from any problem $\min_{Bt=b}\norm{t}_0$ with $B\in\R^{m_0\times N}$. Take $u=v=N$ and $m=m_0+N^2$. 2. Define $\cA(A)=\begin{pmatrix}B\,{\rm diag}(A)\\ A-{\rm Diag}(A)\end{pmatrix}$ and $y=\begin{pmatrix}b\\0\end{pmatrix}$, where ${\rm diag}(A)=(a_{ii})_{i=1}^N$ and ${\rm Diag}(A) = {\rm diag}(a_{11}, \ldots, a_{NN})\in\bR^{N\times N}$. 3. Then $\{A:\cA(A)=y\}$ is the set of **diagonal** matrices whose diagonal $t$ satisfies $Bt=b$, and the rank of a diagonal matrix is the $\ell_0$ "norm" of its diagonal. 4. So a rank-minimization solver also solves $\ell_0$ minimization, through a polynomial-time construction. Since $\ell_0$ minimization is NP-hard, so is rank minimization. . . . ::: {.box-blue style="font-size: 1.15em;"} The affine constraint is easy; the **nonconvex** objective $A\mapsto{\rm rank}(A)$ is the difficulty. **Convex relaxation** replaces it by the "closest convex function". [Can you guess what is the convex relaxation of the rank function (on some set)?]{.blue} ::: ## Convex envelope {.smaller .spread-out} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (convex envelope)" icon=false} Let $C$ be a convex subset of a vector space and $f:C\to\R$. The **convex envelope** ${\rm conv}(f)$ is the largest convex function below $f$ on $C$: for all $x\in C$, $${\rm conv}(f)(x)=\sup\big(g(x):g\text{ convex},\ g\leq f\text{ on }C\big).$$ ::: :::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: center;"} ::: {.column width="55%"} In a Hilbert space $H$, it suffices to take **affine** minorants: $${\rm conv}(f)(x)=\sup_{a\in H,\,b\in\R}\big(\inr{a,x}+b:\ \inr{a,y}+b\leq f(y),\ \forall y\in C\big).$$ ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Any convex function is a maximal function of affine functions](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/convex_fct_maximal_linear_fct-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Fenchel transform {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Fenchel transform)" icon=false} For $f:C\to\R$ with $C\subset H$ a convex set, **the Fenchel transform** of $f$ is $$f^*: y\in H \to \sup_{x\in C}\big(\inr{x,y}-f(x)\big).$$ ::: *Note:* $f^*$ is defined over the entire space $H$ even though $f$ may only be defined over $C$. :::{.box-green} **Exercise:** Show that $f^*$ is convex (even when $f$ is not). ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise:** (Negative entropy): Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be the univariate negative entropy function defined by: $$ f(x) = \begin{cases} x \ln(x) & \text{if } x > 0, \\ 0 & \text{if } x = 0, \\ +\infty & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases} $$ Show that $f^*(y) = e^{y-1}$ for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$. ::: ## Geometric interpretation of the Fenchel transform {center="true"} :::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: center;"} ::: {.column width="50%"} :::{.box-blue style="font-size: 1.10em;"} Given a slope $y\in H$, the Fenchel transform finds the intercept of the largest affine function with slope $y$ below the graph of $f$. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/fenchel-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## The biconjugate function ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (biconjugate)" icon=false style="font-size: 0.8em;"} The **biconjugate** of $f$ is the function $f^{**}:x\in H\to\sup_{y\in H}\big(\inr{x,y}-f^*(y)\big).$ ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow style="font-size: 0.92em;"} **Ex.1:** Compute the biconjugate of the negative entropy function. . . . **Ex.2:** Let $f : x\in \mathbb{R} \to (|x| - 1)^2$ be the double-well function. - Show that $f$ is not convex and draw its convex envelope. - The Fenchel conjugate is $f^*(y)=|y| + \frac{y^2}{4}$ for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$ and the Fenchel biconjugate is $f^{**}(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x| \leq 1, \\ (|x| - 1)^2 & \text{if } |x| > 1. \end{cases}$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. - Draw the Fenchel biconjugate $f$ and make a conjecture about the convex envelope of $f$. ::: ## Convex envelope = biconjugate {.smaller .spread-out} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem" icon=false} Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, $C\subset H$ convex and $f:C\to\R$. Then, $$\forall x\in C, f^{**}(x)={\rm conv}(f)(x).$$ ::: . . . **Proof.** 1. For a fixed slope $y\in H$, the affine function $\inr{y,\cdot}+b$ is below $f$ on $C$ iff $b\leq f(x)-\inr{y,x}$ for all $x\in C$. . . . 2. The best intercept is $b=\inf_{x\in C}\big(f(x)-\inr{y,x}\big)=-f^*(y)$. . . . 3. Hence ${\rm conv}(f)(x)=\sup_{y\in H}\big(\inr{y,x}-f^*(y)\big)=f^{**}(x)$. . . .
::: {.box-green style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.10em;"} **Idea:** To find the convex envelope of the rank function, it suffices to compute its biconjugate. ::: ## The nuclear norm is the convex envelope of the rank {.spread-out} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem" icon=false} The convex envelope of the rank function on $B_{S_\infty}=\{A\in\R^{u\times v}:\norm{A}_{S_\infty}\leq1\}$ is the nuclear norm $\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}$. ::: - The matrix analog of "$\ell_1$ is the convex envelope of $\ell_0$ on $B_\infty^N$". - The dictionary between 'vectors' and 'matrices' goes through the spectrum: $${\rm rank}(A)=\norm{\sigma_A}_{\ell_0},\qquad\norm{A}_{S_1}=\norm{\sigma_A}_{\ell_1},\qquad\norm{A}_{S_\infty}=\norm{\sigma_A}_{\ell_\infty}.$$ - The key tool for reducing matrix problems to problems on spectra is **von Neumann's inequality**. ## von Neumann's inequality ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition (von Neumann's inequality)" style="font-size: 0.8em;" icon=false} For $A,B\in\R^{u\times v}$, $$|\inr{A,B}|\leq\sum_i\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B).$$ Equality $\inr{A,B}=\sum_i\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)$ holds iff, for an SVD $A=U_AD_AV_A^\top$, one has $U_A^\top BV_A=D_B$. Likewise, $\norm{A-B}_{S_2}\geq\norm{\sigma_A-\sigma_B}_2$, with equality when $B=U_AD_BV_A^\top$. ::: - Rank, Schatten norms and $B_{S_\infty}$ are invariant under $A\mapsto UAV$ with $U\in\cO(u)$, $V\in\cO(v)$. - In a supremum over such sets, one can **align the singular vectors** of $B$ with those of $A$, which reduces the problem to vectors via matrices' spectra. ## Proof sketch: biconjugate of the rank {.smaller} Let $f={\rm rank}$ on $B_{S_\infty}$ and $q=u\wedge v$. . . . 1. **Fenchel transform.** By von Neumann's inequality and orthogonal invariance, splitting $B_{S_\infty}$ according to the rank $r$ of $B$: $$f^*(A)=\max_{0\leq r\leq q}\ \sup_{B\in B_{S_\infty},\,{\rm rank}(B)=r}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)-r\Big)=\max_{0\leq r\leq q}\sum_{i=1}^r\big(\sigma_i(A)-1\big)=\sum_{i=1}^q\big(\sigma_i(A)-1\big)_+.$$ . . . 2. **Biconjugate, $\norm{A}_{S_\infty}\leq1$.** Then $f^*(A)=0$, and for $B\in B_{S_\infty}$, $$\sup_{\norm{A}_{S_\infty}\leq1}\sum_i\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)=\sum_i\sigma_i(B)=\norm{B}_{S_1}.$$ . . . 3. **Biconjugate, $\norm{A}_{S_\infty}>1$.** Since $\sigma_i(B)\leq1$, both sums below are nonpositive: $$\sum_i\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)-f^*(A)=\norm{B}_{S_1}+\underbrace{\sum_{\sigma_i(A)\leq1}\big(\sigma_i(A)-1\big)\sigma_i(B)}_{\leq0}+\underbrace{\sum_{\sigma_i(A)>1}\big(\sigma_i(A)-1\big)\big(\sigma_i(B)-1\big)}_{\leq0}\leq\norm{B}_{S_1}.$$ . . . So $f^{**}=\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}$ on $B_{S_\infty}$. $\square$ ## Nuclear norm minimization procedure {.smaller} ::: {.callout-tip title="Key Idea: convex relaxation" icon=false} The nuclear norm is the convex envelope of the rank on $B_{S_\infty}$, so it is natural to replace the (none convex) rank function by the (convex) nuclear norm in the NP-hard rank minimization problem. ::: ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (nuclear norm minimization)" icon=false} With $\cA(A)=(\inr{A,X_i})_{i=1}^m$ and $y=(y_i)_{i=1}^m$, $$\hat A\in\argmin_{A\in\R^{u\times v}}\big(\color{red}{\norm{A}_{S_1}}:\cA(A)=y\big).\tag{NM}$$ ::: - The convex relaxation of rank minimization: the matrix analogue of **Basis Pursuit**. - (NM) is a convex problem. - Basis Pursuit was rewritten as a **linear program**. (NM) can likewise be rewritten as a **semidefinite program** (SDP). ## Semidefinite programs in standard form {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition -- semidefinite program (SDP)" icon=false} An optimization problem is a **semidefinite program** if it can be written as $$\min_{X\in\cS^p}\Big(\inr{C,X}:\tilde\cA(X)=b,\ X\succeq0\Big),$$ where $C\in\cS^p$, $\tilde\cA:\cS^p\to\R^m$ is linear and $b\in\R^m$. ::: We write (NM) in this form, with variable $M$ such that $$ M=\begin{bmatrix}Y&X\\X^\top&Z\end{bmatrix}\in\cS^{u+v}, C=I_{u+v} $$ so $\inr{C,M}={\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)$ and $\tilde\cA(M)=\cA(X) , b=y.$ ::: {style="height: 30px;"} ::: ::: {.box-yellow} - Like linear programs, SDPs are solved approximately by primal–dual barrier methods (e.g. `cvxopt.solvers.conelp`). - however, SDP solvers are **expensive in high dimension**: this motivates the gradient methods of the next part. ::: ## Nuclear norm minimization as an SDP problem We define the (SDP) problem as $$\min_{X\in\R^{u\times v},\,Y\in\cS^u,\,Z\in\cS^v}{\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)\quad\text{such that}\quad\cA(X)=y,\quad\begin{bmatrix}Y&X\\X^\top&Z\end{bmatrix}\succeq0$$ (*Note:* (SDP) is a semidefinite program) ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem: (NM) and (SDP) are equivalent:" icon=false style="font-size: 0.9em;"} 1. if $\hat A$ solves (NM), then $(\hat A,\hat Y,\hat Z)$ solves (SDP) for some $\hat Y,\hat Z$ depending only on $\hat A$; 2. if $(\hat X,\hat Y,\hat Z)$ solves (SDP), then $\hat X$ solves (NM). ::: ## Proof sketch: the SDP lemma ::: {.callout-note title="Lemma" icon=false} Let $A\in\R^{u\times v}$ and $t\geq0$. Then $\norm{A}_{S_1}\leq t$ iff there exist $Y\in\cS^u$ and $Z\in\cS^v$ such that $${\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)\leq2t\qquad\text{and}\qquad\begin{bmatrix}Y&A\\A^\top&Z\end{bmatrix}\succeq0.$$ ::: ## Proof sketch {.smaller} The lemma gives $\min_{Y,Z}\frac12\big({\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)\big)=\norm{X}_{S_1}$ for every feasible $X$, hence the theorem. **($\Leftarrow$)** Take an SVD $A=UDV^\top$ and $I_{u,v}={\rm diag}(1,\ldots,1)\in\R^{u\times v}$. . . . 1. The matrix $M=\begin{bmatrix}I_u&-UI_{u,v}V^\top\\-VI_{u,v}^\top U^\top&I_v\end{bmatrix}$ is positive semidefinite, since $$(x^\top,y^\top)\,M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\norm{x}_2^2+\norm{y}_2^2-2\inr{U^\top x,I_{u,v}V^\top y}\geq0.$$ 2. The trace of a product of two positive semidefinite matrices is nonnegative, so $$0\leq{\rm Tr}\Big(M\begin{bmatrix}Y&A\\A^\top&Z\end{bmatrix}\Big)={\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)-2{\rm Tr}(D),\quad\text{hence}\quad2t\geq2\norm{A}_{S_1}.$$ . . . **($\Rightarrow$)** Take a compact SVD $A=U_rD_rV_r^\top$, with $r={\rm rank}(A)$. 3. Set $Y=U_rD_rU_r^\top+\gamma I_u$ and $Z=V_rD_rV_r^\top+\gamma I_v$, with $\gamma=2(t-\norm{A}_{S_1})/(u+v)$, so that ${\rm Tr}(Y)+{\rm Tr}(Z)=2t$. 4. Then $$\begin{bmatrix}Y&A\\A^\top&Z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}U_r\\V_r\end{bmatrix}D_r\begin{bmatrix}U_r^\top&V_r^\top\end{bmatrix}+\gamma I_{u+v}\succeq0.\qquad\square$$ ## Sparse vectors $\leftrightarrow$ low-rank matrices ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: | | Sparse vectors (CS) | Low-rank matrices (MC) | |:--|:--|:--| | Unknown | $x^*\in\R^N$ | $A^*\in\R^{u\times v}$ | | Structure | $\norm{x^*}_0\leq s$ | ${\rm rank}(A^*)=\norm{\sigma_{A^*}}_0\leq r$ | | Nonconvex procedure | $\ell_0$ minimization (NP-hard) | rank minimization (NP-hard) | | Convex envelope | $\norm{\cdot}_1$ on $B_\infty^N$ | $\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}$ on $B_{S_\infty}$ | | Convex procedure | Basis Pursuit | Nuclear norm minimization | | Implementation | linear program | semidefinite program | | Gaussian measurements | $m\gtrsim s\log(eN/s)$ | $m\gtrsim r(u+v)$ | : {tbl-colwidths="[27, 33, 39]"} # First order algorithms for Matrix Completion ::: {style="height: 70px;"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: avoid SDP via first order methods" icon=false style="font-size: 0.9em;"} The SDP reformulation is hard to solve in high dimension. Here, we build first order algorithms to bypass this limitation. ::: ## The mask operator $P_\Omega$ {.spaced-list} - Each observation reveals one entry of the matrix: a **mask** $$P_\Omega:\R^{u\times v}\to\R^{u\times v},\qquad\big(P_\Omega(A)\big)_{ij}=\begin{cases}A_{ij}&\text{if }(i,j)\in\Omega,\\0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$ where $\Omega\subset\{1,\ldots,u\}\times\{1,\ldots,v\}$ is the set of revealed entries. - $P_\Omega$ is a projection ($P_\Omega^2=P_\Omega$) and is self-adjoint ($P_\Omega^\top=P_\Omega$). - We observe $P_\Omega(A^*)$ and assume that $A^*$ has **low rank**. ## Two procedures: :::{.box-yellow} **Rank-constrained least squares:** $$ \tilde A\in\argmin_{{\rm rank}(A)\leq r}\norm{P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)}_{S_2} $$ ::: :::{.box-yellow} **Nuclear-norm-penalized least squares:** $$\bar A\in\argmin_{A\in\bR^{u\times v}}\Big(\frac12\norm{P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)}_{S_2}^2+\lambda\norm{A}_{S_1}\Big)$$ ::: ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: :::{.box-blue style="font-size: 0.9em;"} Both combine a **data-fidelity term** $A\mapsto\norm{P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)}_{S_2}$ with a rank constraint or a nuclear norm regularization. ::: ## Projected gradient for the rank constraint procedure - $F(A)=\frac12\norm{P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)}_{S_2}^2$ is convex and differentiable, with $$\nabla F(A)=-P_\Omega^\top\big(P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)\big)=P_\Omega(A)-P_\Omega(A^*).$$ - The constraint $\{{\rm rank}(A)\leq r\}$ is **not convex**, but we can still project onto it (next slide). . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (projected gradient descent)" style="font-size: 0.9em;" icon=false} With step sizes $(\gamma_k)_k$, $$A^{k+1}=\color{red}{S_r^{hard}}\Big(A^k+\gamma_k\big(P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A^k)\big)\Big),$$ where $S_r^{hard}$ keeps the $r$ largest singular values and sets the others to $0$. ::: ## Projection onto matrices of rank at most $r$ {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false style="font-size: 0.85em;"} Let $A\in\bR^{u\times v}$ and $r\geq0$. Let $A=PDQ^\top$ be an SVD of $A$, with $D={\rm diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{u\wedge v})$ and $\sigma_1\geq\sigma_2\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{u\wedge v}\geq0$. A projection of $A$ onto $\{B:{\rm rank}(B)\leq r\}$ in $\norm{\cdot}_{S_2}$ is $$\color{red}{S_r^{hard}}(A) = PD_rQ^\top,\qquad D_r={\rm diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r,0,\ldots,0).$$ It is the unique projection when $\sigma_r>\sigma_{r+1}$. ::: . . . **Proof.** 1. von Neumann: $\norm{A-B}_{S_2}\geq\norm{\sigma_A-\sigma_B}_2$, with equality for $B=P\,{\rm diag}(\sigma_B)Q^\top$. 2. If ${\rm rank}(B)\leq r$, then $\norm{\sigma_A-\sigma_B}_2^2\geq\sum_{j>r}\sigma_j(A)^2$, with equality for $\sigma_B=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r,0,\ldots,0)$. $\square$ . . . ::: {style="height: 40px;"} ::: :::{.box-green} - $S_r^{hard}(\cdot)$ is called the **hard thresholding spectral operator**. - Its `only` costs one SVD (and only the $r$ leading singular triplets are needed). - It is a special case where one can solve efficiently a non-convex optimization problem. ::: ## The subdifferential of a convex function {.smaller} **Aim:** Construct a first order algorithm for the nuclear norm penalized least squares procedure. **Problem:** The nuclear norm is not differentiable. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Subdifferential)" icon=false} Let $f:C\to\R$ be a convex function (on a convex set $C\subset\R^n$). Let $x\in C$. The **Subdifferential of $f$ in $x$** is the set $$\partial^-f(x)=\big\{g\in\R^n:f(y)\geq f(x)+\inr{g,y-x},\ \forall y\in C\big\}.$$ Its elements are called the **subgradients**. ::: . . . :::{.box-green} - **Exercise 1:** Show that if $f$ is a convex function that is differentiable at $x\in \overset{\circ}{A}$ then $\partial^-f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}$. - **Exercise 2:** Compute the subdifferential of the absolute function $t\to|t|$ at all points of $\bR$. - **Exercise 3:** Let $f$ be a convex function on an open convex set $C\subset\R^n$: show that $x^*$ is solution to $\min_{x\in C}f(x)$ iff $0\in \partial^-f(x^*)$. - **Exercise 4:** Compute the subdifferential of the Euclidean norm over $\mathbb{R}^p$. ::: ## Proximal operators {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (proximal operator)" icon=false} For a convex function $g:\R^n\to\R$, $${\rm prox}_g(x)=\argmin_{u\in\R^n}\Big(\frac12\norm{u-x}_2^2+g(u)\Big).$$ ::: ::: {style="height: 30px;"} ::: :::{.box-green} - **Exercise 1:** Let $K$ be a non-empty closed and convex set and denote by $i_K$ its indicator function ($0$ on $K$, $+\infty$ outside). Then for all $\gamma>0$, ${\rm prox}_{\gamma i_C}(x) = P_C(x)$, where $P_K$ is the projection operator over $K$. - **Exercise 2:** Let $f(u)=|u|$ and let $\gamma > 0$. Show that ${\rm prox}_{\gamma f}(x) = {\rm sign}(x) \max(|x| - \gamma, 0)$ and draw the proximal map of $f$. ::: ::: {style="height: 40px;"} ::: :::{.box-red} **Proximal operators generalize projections:** For $K$ be a non-empty closed and convex set: for all $x\in\R^n$, $${\rm proj}_K(x)={\rm prox}_{i_K}(x).$$ ::: ## Proximal maps of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_0$ {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="58%"} The objective functions are **separable**: \begin{align*} \frac12\norm{u-z}_2^2+\gamma\norm{u}_{\color{blue}{1}}&=\sum_j\Big(\frac12(u_j-z_j)^2+\gamma|u_j|\Big)\\ \frac12\norm{u-z}_2^2+\gamma\norm{u}_{\color{blue}{0}}&=\sum_j\Big(\frac12(u_j-z_j)^2+\gamma I(u_j\neq 0)\Big) \end{align*} ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Soft thresholding (left) and hard thresholding (right) at level $\gamma$.](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/thresholding-1.svg){fig-align='right' width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::: Scalar problems: for all $s\in\R$, $$ \argmin_{t\in\R}\left[\frac12(s-t)^2+\gamma|t|\right] ={\rm sgn}(s)\big(|s|-\gamma\big)_+ \text{ and } \argmin_{t\in\R}\left[\frac12(s-t)^2+\gamma I(t\neq 0)\right] =s\,I(|s|\geq \sqrt{2\gamma}). $$ ::: {style="height: 30px;"} ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition (proximal maps of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_0$): For all $z\in\R^N$:" icon=false} :::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"} ::: {.column width="50%"} - **soft thresholding:** ${\rm prox}_{\gamma\norm{\cdot}_1}(z)=\big({\rm sgn}(z_j)(|z_j|-\gamma)_+\big)_{j=1}^N$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} - **hard thresholding:** ${\rm prox}_{(\gamma^2/2)\norm{\cdot}_0}(z)=\big(z_j\,I(|z_j|\geq\gamma)\big)_{j=1}^N$. ::: :::: ::: ## Fixed-point characterization of proximal gradient descent {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Let $f:\R^n\to\R$ be [convex and differentiable]{.blue}, $g:\R^n\to\R$ [convex]{.blue}, and $\gamma>0$. Then $$x^*\in\argmin_{x\in\R^n}\big(f(x)+g(x)\big)\iff x^*={\rm prox}_{\gamma g}\big(x^*-\gamma\nabla f(x^*)\big).$$ ::: **Proof.** 1. Replacing $(f,g)$ by $(\gamma f,\gamma g)$, we may take $\gamma=1$. 2. By the optimality condition for the prox: $\ u^*={\rm prox}_g(z)\iff z-u^*\in\partial^-g(u^*)$. 3. So $x^*={\rm prox}_g\big(x^*-\nabla f(x^*)\big)\iff-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial^-g(x^*)\iff0\in\nabla f(x^*)+\partial^-g(x^*)$. . . . ::: {style="height: 30px;"} ::: :::{.box-red} A solution to the problem $\min_{x\in\R^n}\big(f(x)+g(x)\big)$ is a fixed point of $G:x\mapsto{\rm prox}_{\gamma g}\big(x-\gamma\nabla f(x)\big)$. We can use a **fixed point algorithm** to approximate it: $\color{red}{x_{k+1}=G(x_k)}$, possibly with varying steps $\gamma_k$. ::: ## Prox of the nuclear norm: soft spectral thresholding {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Let $\gamma>0$ and let $A=UDV^\top$ be an SVD of $A$. Then $${\rm prox}_{\gamma\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}}(A)=S_\gamma^{soft}(A)=UD_\gamma V^\top,\qquad D_\gamma={\rm diag}\big((\sigma_1-\gamma)_+,\ldots,(\sigma_{u\wedge v}-\gamma)_+\big).$$ ::: **Proof.** 1. von Neumann: $\norm{A-B}_{S_2}^2=\norm{A}_{S_2}^2+\norm{B}_{S_2}^2-2\inr{A,B}\geq\norm{\sigma_A-\sigma_B}_2^2$, with equality for $B=U\,{\rm diag}(\sigma_B)V^\top$. 2. So the prox has the form $U{\rm diag}(\hat d)V^\top$, with $\hat d={\rm prox}_{\gamma\norm{\cdot}_1}(\sigma_A)$. 3. Since $\sigma_A\geq0$, soft thresholding gives $\hat d=\big((\sigma_i-\gamma)_+\big)_i$. $\square$ . . . ::: {style="height: 60px;"} ::: :::{.box-green} **Exercise:** Construct a proximal gradient descent algorithm for matrix completion. ::: ## Proximal gradient descent for matrix completion {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (proximal gradient descent)" icon=false} For $\min_A\big(\frac12\norm{P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A)}_{S_2}^2+\lambda\norm{A}_{S_1}\big)$, with step sizes $(\gamma_k)_k$: $$A_{k+1}=S_{\lambda\gamma_k}^{soft}\Big(A_k+\gamma_k\big(P_\Omega(A^*)-P_\Omega(A_k)\big)\Big).$$ ::: - Same cost for both methods: no SDP, but one SVD (or a truncated SVD) per iteration, which can still be expensive. ::: {style="height: 40px;"} ::: | Problem | Method | Spectral step | |:--|:--|:--| | ${\rm rank}(A)\leq r$ | projected gradient | hard: keep $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r$ | | $+\lambda\norm{A}_{S_1}$ | proximal gradient | soft: $\sigma_i\mapsto(\sigma_i-\lambda\gamma_k)_+$ | ::: {style="height: 60px;"} ::: ::: {.box-green} **Key Idea: thresholding the spectrum:** Projecting onto low-rank matrices and computing the prox of the nuclear norm give two first order methods for matrix completion by projected or proximal gradient descent. ::: ## Matrix completion on pictures via SDP and proximal gradient descent ::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; height: 450px;"} ::: {.box-green style="text-align: center; max-width: 850px; width: 100%;"} Open the notebook `lab_mat_completion.ipynb` ::: ::: :::{.box-yellow} - Check that real images have low rank. - Use an SDP solver to complete a matrix. - Implement a proximal gradient descent algorithm for matrix completion. ::: # Matrix Factorization and Metadata for Recommender Systems ## A latent space for users and items :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - Represent users **and** items in the same **latent space** $\R^d$: - $p_i\in\R^d$ represents user $i$; - $q_j\in\R^d$ represents item $j$. - The inner product ${\color{red}{\inr{p_i,q_j}}}$ measures the **affinity** between user $i$ and item $j$. - Users close to an item in the latent space are likely to appreciate it. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![Latent space $\R^2$ for the Netflix data: users and movies are represented in the same place.](images/latent_space.png){width="95%"} ::: :::: ## Factorization of the users/items matrix {.smaller} - Data: $\{(user_i,item_j,grade_{ij}):(i,j)\in\Omega\}$. - Build $(p_i)_{i\leq u}$ and $(q_j)_{j\leq v}$ so that ${\color{red}{\inr{p_i,q_j}\approx grade_{ij}}}$ for every $(i,j)\in\Omega$. - The values $\inr{p_i,q_j}$ for $(i,j)\notin\Omega$ **complete** the matrix. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Factorizing $A^*\approx PQ$, with $P\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times d}$ (rows $p_i^\top$) and $Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times v}$ (columns $q_j$).](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/factorization-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Key Idea: low rank made explicit" icon=false} ${\rm rank}(PQ)\leq d$. Approximating $A^*$ by $PQ$ approximates it by a low-rank matrix, which only works if $A^*$ is approximately low rank. ::: ::: :::: ## Regularized least-squares objective - Fit the observed entries: $$\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega}\big(grade_{ij}-\inr{p_i,q_j}\big)^2=\norm{P_\Omega(A^*-PQ)}_2^2,\qquad P=(p_i^\top)_{i\leq u},\ Q=(q_j)_{j\leq v}.$$ - $PQ$ is invariant under $(P,Q)\mapsto(\alpha P,Q/\alpha)$, so we also penalize the norms: $$f(P,Q)=\frac12\norm{P_\Omega(A^*-PQ)}_2^2+\lambda\big(\norm{P}_2^2+\norm{Q}_2^2\big),\qquad\lambda>0.$$ . . . - $f$ is **not jointly convex** in $(P,Q)$, but it is convex in each block: $$\partial_1f(P,Q)=-P_\Omega(A^*-PQ)\,Q^\top+2\lambda P,\qquad\partial_2f(P,Q)=-P^\top P_\Omega(A^*-PQ)+2\lambda Q.$$ ## Alternating gradient descent {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (alternating gradient descent, ARLS)" icon=false} **Data:** $\{A^*_{ij}:(i,j)\in\Omega\}$. **Init:** $P_0\in\R^{u\times d}$, $Q_0\in\R^{d\times v}$, step sizes $(\eta_k)_k$ and $(\mu_k)_k$. **While** the stopping criterion is not met: 1. $P_{k+1}=P_k-\eta_k\,\partial_1f(P_k,Q_k)$ 2. $Q_{k+1}=Q_k-\mu_k\,\partial_2f(P_{k+1},Q_k)$ **Output:** $P\in\R^{u\times d}$ and $Q\in\R^{d\times v}$ such that $A^*\approx PQ$. ::: - ARLS stands for **Alternating Ridge Least Squares**: each block update is a ridge-regularized least-squares step. - To recommend, compute $PQ$ and pick the largest entries on each row. ## Clustering users and items in the latent space :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - The rows of $P$ represent the **users** and the columns of $Q$ the **items**. - Clustering the rows of $P$ gives groups of users with the same tastes. - Clustering the columns of $Q$ gives groups of similar items. - The latent space is useful **beyond recommendation**. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Users (blue triangles) and items (red squares) in the latent space form clusters.](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/latent-clusters-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) {.smaller} - In plain factorization, $\inr{p_i,q_j}$ can be **negative**. One option is to map negative values to the lowest rating ($1$ for Netflix). - Another is to impose **nonnegative** latent coordinates: $$\min_{P\in\R^{u\times d},\,Q\in\R^{d\times v}}\Big(\norm{P_\Omega(A^*-PQ)}_2:\ P\geq0,\ Q\geq0\Big)\qquad(P\geq0\text{ means }P_{ij}\geq0\ \forall i,j).$$ . . . - Still convex in each block. Respect the constraints by **projected gradient** (or conditional gradient, i.e. Frank–Wolfe). The projection is easy: ${\rm proj}(P)=(\max(P_{ij},0))_{i,j}$. ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (alternating projected gradient descent)" icon=false} **While** the stopping criterion is not met: 1. $P_{k+1}={\rm proj}\big(P_k-\eta_k\,\partial_1f(P_k,Q_k)\big)$ 2. $Q_{k+1}={\rm proj}\big(Q_k-\mu_k\,\partial_2f(P_{k+1},Q_k)\big)$ ::: - Other NMF algorithms: Lee and Seung, NIPS 2001. ## Adding metadata to matrix factorization {.smaller} **Metadata** are additional data beyond the ratings: - $x_i$: feature vector of user $i$ (age, sex, socio-professional category; via one-hot encoding, embedding or autoencoding); - $z_j$: feature vector of item $j$ (price, categories, and so on); - $U\in\R^{u\times u}$: users/users matrix of influences (likes, positive messages, retweets); - $I\in\R^{v\times v}$: items/items matrix of affinities (cast, producer, release year, genre). . . . **Linear model:** for $(i,j)\in\Omega$, $$A^*_{ij}\approx\inr{p_i,q_j}+\underbrace{(a_i+\inr{b_i,x_i})}_{\text{user features}}+\underbrace{(c_j+\inr{d_j,z_j})}_{\text{item features}}+\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{r=1}^uU_{ir}\inr{p_r,q_j}}_{\text{influence of other users}}+\underbrace{\beta\sum_{s=1}^vI_{js}\inr{p_i,q_s}}_{\text{similar items}}.$$ - If user $r$ influences $i$ ($U_{ir}\gg0$) and $r$ likes $j$ ($\inr{p_r,q_j}\gg0$), the predicted rating of $j$ by $i$ increases. - We take $U_{ii}=0$ and $I_{jj}=0$, so that $\inr{p_i,q_j}$ is not counted twice. ## Learning model's parameters - **Parameters:** the latent vectors $(p_i)_i$, $(q_j)_j$ and the coefficients $a_i,b_i,c_j,d_j$. - Minimize the regularized squared error $$ F\big((p_i), (q_j), (a_i), (b_i), (c_j), (d_j)\big)= \\ \sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega}\Big[A^*_{ij}-\Big(\inr{p_i,q_j}+(a_i+\inr{b_i,x_i})+(c_j+\inr{d_j,z_j})\\ +\alpha\sum_rU_{ir}\inr{p_r,q_j}+\beta\sum_sI_{js}\inr{p_i,q_s}\Big)\Big]^2+\lambda\Big(\sum_i\norm{p_i}_2^2+\sum_j\norm{q_j}_2^2\Big). $$ . . . - **Alternate** minimizations in $(p_i)_i$ and in $(q_j)_j$, as in ARLS, and update $a_i,b_i,c_j,d_j$ at each iteration. - For fixed $(p_i)$ and $(q_j)$, minimizing in $(a_i,b_i,c_j,d_j)$ is an explicit **least-squares** problem. - Instead of the $\ell_2$ penalty, one can impose positivity of the $p_i$ and $q_j$, as in NMF. # Benchmark Approaches: Collaborative and Content-Based Filtering ## Two benchmark families :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - The previous approaches encode the **low-rank** structure of $A^*$. - Older and more natural algorithms rely directly on **similarities**. Any new recommender system must be compared with these **benchmarks**. - They are the simplest to understand and implement, and the fastest to run. 1. **Collaborative filtering:** similarity between **users**. 2. **Content-based filtering:** similarity between **items**. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![Collaborative filtering uses similarities between users; content-based filtering uses similarities between items.](images/benchmark_filtering.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: ## Similarity-weighted completion {.smaller} - Everything rests on a similarity measure ${\rm sim}(i,i')$ between users $i,i'\in[u]$, or ${\rm sim}(j,j')$ between items $j,j'\in[v]$. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (benchmark predictors)" icon=false} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Collaborative filtering:** $$\hat A_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{i'\in[u]}{\rm sim}(i,i')\,\hat A_{i'j}}{\sum_{i'\in[u]}{\rm sim}(i,i')}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Content-based filtering:** $$\hat A_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{j'\in[v]}{\rm sim}(j,j')\,\hat A_{ij'}}{\sum_{j'\in[v]}{\rm sim}(j,j')}$$ ::: :::: ::: - These formulas are implicit and suggest an iterative algorithm. Usually a **single step** is performed, summing only over observed entries $A^*_{i'j}$ (resp. $A^*_{ij'}$) with indices in $\Omega$. - Metadata (on users, items, user/user or item/item relations) enter naturally through the similarity. ## Cosine similarity {.smaller} - For two users $i,i'\in[u]$, let $N(i,i')=\{j\in[v]:(i,j)\in\Omega\text{ and }(i',j)\in\Omega\}$ be the items rated by both. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (cosine similarity)" icon=false} $${\rm sim}(i,i')=\frac{\sum_{j\in N(i,i')}A^*_{ij}A^*_{i'j}}{\sqrt{\sum_{j\in N(i,i')}(A^*_{ij})^2}\ \sqrt{\sum_{j\in N(i,i')}(A^*_{i'j})^2}}$$ ::: - The cosine of the angle between the masked rating rows $(P_\Omega A^*)_{i\bullet}$ and $(P_\Omega A^*)_{i'\bullet}$, restricted to their common items. - A cosine similarity between items is defined in the same way, on the columns. # Recommender Systems via Deep Learning ## Users and items embeddings :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **Neural Collaborative Filtering** (NCF) elaborates on matrix factorization: users and items are **embedded**, possibly in two different latent spaces, and the rating is predicted by a function more complex than an inner product. - An **embedding layer** is a linear map from the one-hot vector $e_i\in\R^u$ of user $i$ to $\R^d$: it has $u\times d$ weights to learn. - Embeddings can be designed by hand ("featuring"), given by a kernel, or **learned** from the data, as $p_i$ and $q_j$ in matrix factorization. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![Users embedding: one-hot encoding in $\mathbb{R}^u$ mapped to the latent space $\mathbb{R}^d$.](images/users_embedding.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: ## Fully connected layers :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} - A **fully connected** (dense) layer with $m$ inputs and $p$ outputs has a weight matrix $W=(w_{ij})_{i\leq p,\,j\leq m}$ and maps $x\in\R^m$ to $y\in\R^p$: $$y_i=\sigma\big(w_{i1}x_1+\cdots+w_{im}x_m\big),\qquad i\in[p].$$ - **Activation** $\sigma$: sigmoid $t\mapsto(1+e^{-t})^{-1}$, or ReLU $t\mapsto\max(0,t)$. - **Structure agnostic:** the layer of choice when nothing is known about the structure of the problem. - It has the maximal number of weights, so training is expensive, and it is usually less efficient than layers designed for a structured problem. ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![A fully connected layer with $9$ inputs and $5$ outputs: $45$ weights.](images/fully_connected_layer.png){width="80%"} ::: :::: ## Stacking fully connected layers - Stacking fully connected layers lets the network learn **complicated dependencies** between inputs and outputs. ![A network of $4$ fully connected layers: $8$ inputs, three hidden layers of $9$ neurons, $4$ outputs.](images/fully_connected_stack.png){width="35%" fig-align="center"} - Number of weights (without biases): $8\times9+9\times9+9\times9+9\times4=270$. ## Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} - **Input:** a (user, item) pair. - **Embedding layer** for the user and for the item, followed by a **fully connected** network. - **Output:** the probabilities of the two classes "interaction" ($1$) and "no interaction" ($0$). - The predicted class is the most probable one: here class $1$, since $0.8>0.2$. ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ![NCF architecture: an embedding layer followed by a fully connected network.](images/architecture_dl_rs.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: ## Binary cross-entropy loss {.smaller} - Training data: a batch $(user_i,item_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N$, with $y_i\in\{0,1\}$. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (binary cross-entropy)" icon=false} $$BCE(\hat y,y)=-\sum_{i=1}^N\Big(y_i\log\hat y_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat y_i)\Big),$$ where $\hat y_i$ is the network's prediction for the input $(user_i,item_i)$. ::: - The loss depends on all the network weights $w$: $\ BCE(\hat y,y)=f\big(w,(user_i,item_i)_{i=1}^N\big)=f(w)$. - Learn $\hat w$ by minimizing $w\mapsto f(w)$ with a gradient-type method. - Then complete the matrix by querying $f\big(\hat w,(user_i,item_j)\big)$ for every $(i,j)\notin\Omega$. ## ADAM and backpropagation {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (ADAM, adaptive moment estimation)" icon=false} Set $m_0=v_0=0$ and choose $\beta_1,\beta_2,\eta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. At step $k$: 1. Moments: $\ m_k=\beta_1m_{k-1}+(1-\beta_1)\nabla f(w^{(k)})$ and $v_k=\beta_2v_{k-1}+(1-\beta_2)\big(\nabla f(w^{(k)})\big)^2$ (coordinatewise). 2. Bias correction: $\ \hat m_k=m_k/(1-\beta_1^k)$ and $\hat v_k=v_k/(1-\beta_2^k)$. 3. Update: $\ w^{(k+1)}=w^{(k)}-\dfrac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat v_k}+\varepsilon}\,\hat m_k$. ::: - ADAM is a **first-order** method: everything rests on computing $\nabla f$ efficiently, for a function of many weights. - **Backpropagation**, from automatic differentiation, computes these gradients mainly through the **chain rule**. It is used by every solver, including ADAM. ## Hyperparameters and best practices {.smaller} - Many hyperparameters must be chosen: - number of layers and number of neurons; - dimensions of the embedding spaces; - number of **epochs** (full passes over the database, split into batches); - batch size; - learning rate $\eta$. - Cross-validation would be the logical choice, but training a single network is already too costly. . . . ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} In practice one follows **best practices** from experts. For example: batch size $512$, $5$ epochs, and a dense network with $16$ input neurons, $64$ intermediate neurons and $32$ outputs. ::: ## Negative samples - The data are (user, item) **interactions** only: there is no rating and no example of a deliberately avoided item. - An absence of interaction is ambiguous: the user may not know the item, or may not want it. - Without **negative samples**, the network learns to answer $1$ for every (user, item) pair. . . . - **Simplest strategy** (debatable): add, as negatives, random items among those the user has not interacted with. - For example, take $4$ times as many negative samples as positive ones per user, to compensate for their poor quality. - Alternatives: the least popular items of each batch, or more collaborative strategies. ## Dropout :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - Overfitting in neural networks is still poorly understood: networks with zero training error can still generalize well. - **Dropout:** at each gradient step, a random proportion $p$ of the units is dropped. These units are ignored and their weights are not updated at that step. - This adds one hyperparameter, $p$, to be chosen in advance. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014).](images/drop_out.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: # Performance Criteria ## Train/test split :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - From the observed ratings $(A^*_{ij}:(i,j)\in\Omega)$, set aside a percentage as the **test set**. The remaining ratings form the **training set**. - The recommender system is built on the training set only, and evaluated on the test set. - The test entries are **not** drawn completely at random over the matrix: each row (each user) must keep about fifty ratings in the test set. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Observed entries of the users/items matrix split into training (blue) and test (red) entries; every row has test entries.](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/train-test-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Precision, recall and F1 score {.smaller} For each user $i$, let $R_i$ be the set of items **recommended** to $i$ and $T_i$ the set of items that $i$ did appreciate in the **test set**. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (precision, recall, F1 score)" icon=false} $${\rm recall}_i=\frac{|R_i\cap T_i|}{|T_i|},\qquad{\rm precision}_i=\frac{|R_i\cap T_i|}{|R_i|},\qquad F1_i=\frac{2\times{\rm recall}_i\times{\rm precision}_i}{{\rm recall}_i+{\rm precision}_i}.$$ ::: - **Recall:** the proportion of the appreciated items that we recommended. - **Precision:** the proportion of the recommended items that were appreciated. - The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the two: it is high only when both are. - These quantities are computed **per user**. Aggregate them by their mean and quantiles, or plot the distribution of the F1 scores over the users. ## MAE, RMSE and overfitting {.smaller} - Compare the predicted ratings $\hat A_{ij}$ with the test ratings, on the test indices $\Omega_{test}$: $${\rm MAE}=\frac{1}{|\Omega_{test}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega_{test}}\big|\hat A_{ij}-A^*_{ij}\big|,\qquad{\rm RMSE}=\Big(\frac{1}{|\Omega_{test}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega_{test}}\big(\hat A_{ij}-A^*_{ij}\big)^2\Big)^{1/2}.$$ - MAE is an $\ell_1$ distance and RMSE an $\ell_2$ distance. Any distance between estimated and observed test ratings can serve as a criterion. . . . - Compute these criteria on **both** the training and the test sets. A training error much smaller than the test error signals **overfitting**. ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} This diagnosis has recently been called into question: deep networks can make zero error on the training sample and still generalize well, with a reasonable error on the test sample. ::: ## Gradient proximal VS Neural collaborative filtering ::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; height: 550px;"} ::: {.box-green style="text-align: center; max-width: 850px; width: 100%;"} Open the notebook

**Key Idea:** So far, random measurements are the best. ::: ## The exact recovery property $RE(r)$ {.smaller} - **Goal:** for which measurements $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ and which $m$ does (NM) recover **every** matrix of rank $r$? - Write $\Sigma_r=\{A\in\R^{u\times v}:{\rm rank}(A)=r\}$. ::: {.callout-note title="Definition ($RE(r)$)" icon=false} $\cA$ satisfies the **exact recovery property of order $r$** when, for every $A\in\Sigma_r$, $$\argmin_X\big(\norm{X}_{S_1}:\cA(X)=\cA(A)\big)=\{A\}.$$ ::: . . . Two routes: 1. **RIP approach:** matrix versions of NSP and RIP, with the same arguments as for Basis Pursuit. 2. **General approach:** highlights the role of the **nondifferentiability** of the objective function in inducing sparsity. ## The rank Null Space Property {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (rank-NSP)" icon=false} $\cA:\R^{u\times v}\to\R^m$ satisfies the **rank Null Space Property of degree $r$** when, for every $A\in{\rm Ker}(\cA)\setminus\{0\}$, $$\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(A)<\sum_{i\geq r+1}\sigma_i(A).$$ ::: - Vector analogue: $\norm{v_J}_1<\norm{v_{J^c}}_1$ for every $v\in{\rm Ker}(A)\setminus\{0\}$ and $|J|\leq s$. - The $r$ largest **singular values** play the role of the $s$ largest coordinates. - The kernel must contain no matrix whose spectrum is concentrated on a few singular values. ## Rank-NSP is equivalent to exact recovery {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} For a linear operator $\cA:\R^{u\times v}\to\R^m$, $$\cA\text{ satisfies }RE(r)\iff\cA\text{ satisfies rank-NSP}(r).$$ ::: - The arguments are the same as in the vector case, with singular values in place of the absolute values of the coordinates. . . . ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} As in the vector case, the rank-NSP is a necessary and sufficient condition, but it is hard to check directly. We therefore introduce a matrix version of RIP. ::: ## The rank Restricted Isometry Property ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (rank-RIP)" icon=false} $\cA$ satisfies the **rank Restricted Isometry Property of degree $r$**, with isometry constant $\delta_r$, when for every matrix $A$ of rank $r$, $$(1-\delta_r)\norm{A}_{S_2}^2\leq\frac{\norm{\cA(A)}_{\ell_2^m}^2}{m}\leq(1+\delta_r)\norm{A}_{S_2}^2.$$ ::: - $\cA$ has a huge kernel, so it cannot be an isometry on all of $\R^{u\times v}$, only on **low-rank matrices**. - The Frobenius norm $\norm{\cdot}_{S_2}$ plays the role of $\ell_2$. ## Rank-RIP implies rank-NSP ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} There exist absolute constants $c_0>0$ and $00$, let $\cC_{r^*}=\{x\in E:\norm{x}_2\geq r^*\norm{x}\}$. The operator $\cA$ satisfies the **restricted singular value condition of radius $r^*$** when, for every $x\in\cC_{r^*}$, $$\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\inr{x,X_i}^2\geq\frac{\norm{x}_2^2}{2}.$$ ::: - The cone $\cC_{r^*}$ contains the "sparse" directions, where $\norm{x}_2$ is large compared with $\norm{x}$. - For $\ell_1$ on $\R^N$, $VSR(r^*)$ is implied by $RIP(s)$ with $r^*\sim1/\sqrt s$. - For sub-Gaussian measurements, with probability at least $1-2\exp(-c_0m)$, $VSR(r^*)$ holds for $$r^*=\inf\big(r>0:\ell^*(B\cap rB_2)\leq c_1r\sqrt m\big).$$ ## Gaussian mean width {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Gaussian mean width)" icon=false} Let $T\subset H$ and let $(G_t)_{t\in T}$ be the canonical Gaussian process indexed by $T$. The **Gaussian mean width** of $T$ is $$\ell^*(T)=\E\sup_{t\in T}G_t.$$ ::: - In finite dimension, $G_t=\inr{G,t}$ with $G$ a standard Gaussian vector. In $\R^N$, $$\ell^*(T)=\E\sup_{t\in T}\sum_{j=1}^Ng_jt_j,\qquad g_1,\ldots,g_N\ \text{i.i.d. }\cN(0,1).$$ - $\ell^*$ measures the **complexity** of $T$. The radius $r^*$ is the point where the complexity of $B\cap rB_2$ is balanced by $r\sqrt m$. ## The sparsity parameter $\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)$ {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (sparsity parameter)" icon=false} For $x^*\in E$ and $r^*>0$, $$\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)=\inf_{h\in S\cap r^*B_2}\ \sup_{z\in\partial\norm{\cdot}(x^*)}\inr{z,h}.$$ ::: - For $x^*\neq0$, $\partial\norm{\cdot}(x^*)\subset S_*$, so $\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)\leq1$. - **Condition of interest:** $\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)>0$. Every direction $h\in S\cap r^*B_2$ must be "seen" by some subgradient at $x^*$. - The **larger** the subdifferential, the more likely $\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)>0$. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A poor subdifferential (left) versus a rich one (right). The richness at sparse points, or near them in the noisy case, plays a central role in high-dimensional statistics.](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/subdiff-richness-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Exact recovery theorem {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem" icon=false} Assume that $\cA$ satisfies $VSR(r^*)$ for some $r^*>0$. Then, for every $x^*$ such that $\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)>0$, $$\argmin_{x:\,\cA(x)=\cA(x^*)}\norm{x}=\{x^*\}.$$ ::: **Proof.** Let $x\neq x^*$ with $\cA(x)=\cA(x^*)$, and set $h=x-x^*$. . . . 1. If $h\in\cC_{r^*}$, then $VSR(r^*)$ gives $\norm{\cA(h)}_2^2\geq m\norm{h}_2^2/2>0$, a contradiction. So $h\notin\cC_{r^*}$, i.e. $h/\norm{h}\in S\cap r^*B_2$. . . . 2. For every $g\in\partial\norm{\cdot}(x^*)$: $\ \norm{x}-\norm{x^*}\geq\inr{g,h}=\inr{g,h/\norm{h}}\,\norm{h}$. . . . 3. Taking the supremum over $g$, then the infimum over directions: $\ \norm{x}-\norm{x^*}\geq\Delta_{r^*}(x^*)\norm{h}>0$. $\square$ ## Subdifferential of the $\ell_1$ norm {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="58%"} - Absolute value: $\ \partial|\cdot|(t)=\{1\}$ if $t>0$, $\{-1\}$ if $t<0$, $[-1,1]$ if $t=0$. - In $\R^2$: $\ \partial\norm{\cdot}_1\big((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\big)=\{(1,1)\}$ and $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1\big((1,0)\big)=\{(1,g):|g|\leq1\}$. ::: {.callout-note title="Lemma" icon=false} Let $x^*\in\R^N\setminus\{0\}$ be $s$-sparse, with $I={\rm supp}(x^*)$. Then $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1(x^*)$ is the set of $z\in\R^N$ such that $$z_i={\rm sign}(x^*_i)\ \text{ for } i\in I\qquad\text{and}\qquad|z_i|\leq1\ \text{ for } i\notin I.$$ If $x^*=0$, then $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1(0)=B_\infty^N$. ::: - **Proof:** $g\in S_\infty$ is norming for $x^*$, i.e. $\inr{g,x^*}=\norm{x^*}_1$, iff $g_i={\rm sign}(x^*_i)$ on $I$. The coordinates on $I^c$ are free in $[-1,1]$. - $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1(x^*)$ is a copy of $B_\infty^{N-s}$: **the sparser $x^*$, the richer the subdifferential**. - Extremes: $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1(e_1)=\{1\}\times B_\infty^{N-1}$, whereas $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1\big((1,\ldots,1)\big)=\{(1,\ldots,1)\}$, a point where $\norm{\cdot}_1$ is differentiable. ::: ::: {.column width="42%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Subdifferential of $\|\cdot\|_1$ in dimension $2$ at $(1/2,1/2)^\top$ (a single direction) and at $(1,0)^\top$ (a whole cone).](recommendation_systems_files/figure-revealjs/subdiff-l1-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Subdifferential of the nuclear norm {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem" icon=false} Let $A\in\R^{u\times v}$ ($u\geq v$) have rank $r$, with SVD $A=UDV^\top$ and blocks $$U=\big[U^{(1)}\ U^{(2)}\big]\in\cO(u),\qquad V=\big[V^{(1)}\ V^{(2)}\big]\in\cO(v),\qquad U^{(1)}\in\R^{u\times r},\ V^{(1)}\in\R^{v\times r}.$$ Then $$\partial\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}(A)=\Big\{U^{(1)}{V^{(1)}}^\top+U^{(2)}W{V^{(2)}}^\top:\ W\in\R^{(u-r)\times(v-r)},\ \norm{W}_{S_\infty}\leq1\Big\}.$$ ::: . . . - $U^{(1)}{V^{(1)}}^\top=\sum_{i=1}^ru_iv_i^\top$ plays the role of the **sign** of $A=\sum_i\sigma_iu_iv_i^\top$. - $U^{(2)}W{V^{(2)}}^\top$ lives **off the "support"** of $A$: $\inr{A,U^{(2)}W{V^{(2)}}^\top}=0$ for every $W$. It plays the role of the free coordinates $|z_i|\leq1$, $i\notin I$. - The smaller the rank $r$, the larger the free block $W$, and the **richer** the subdifferential. ## Orthogonally invariant norms {.smaller} - A norm on $\R^{u\times v}$ is **orthogonally invariant** when $\norm{UAV}=\norm{A}$ for all $U\in\cO(u)$, $V\in\cO(v)$. - Then $\norm{A}=\phi(\sigma_A)$ for an **unconditional** norm $\phi$ on $\R^{u\wedge v}$: $\ \phi(\eps_1x_1,\ldots,\eps_{u\wedge v}x_{u\wedge v})=\phi(x)$ for all signs $\eps_i\in\{\pm1\}$. Example: Schatten norms, with $\phi=\ell_p$. ::: {.callout-note title="Lemma" icon=false} For an orthogonally invariant norm $\norm{\cdot}=\phi(\sigma_\cdot)$ and $A\in\R^{u\times v}$, $$\partial\norm{\cdot}(A)={\rm conv}\big\{U\Sigma V^\top:\ A=UDV^\top,\ \Sigma={\rm diag}(\sigma),\ \sigma\in\partial\phi(\sigma_A)\big\},$$ where all SVDs of $A$ are considered. ::: . . . - **$\supseteq$:** for $G$ in the convex hull, $\inr{G,A}=\phi(\sigma_A)=\norm{A}$, and von Neumann's inequality gives $\inr{G,R}\leq1$ whenever $\norm{R}\leq1$. - **$\subseteq$:** by separation of convex sets, comparing two formulas for the directional derivative: $$\lim_{\eps\to0^+}\frac{\norm{A+\eps R}-\norm{A}}{\eps}=\max_{G\in\partial\norm{\cdot}(A)}\inr{R,G}=\max_{d\in\partial\phi(\sigma_A)}\sum_id_i\,u_i^\top Rv_i.$$ ## Proof sketch: subdifferential of the nuclear norm {.smaller} Apply the lemma with $\phi=\norm{\cdot}_1$. . . . 1. $\partial\norm{\cdot}_1(\sigma_A)=\{g:g_i=1\text{ for }i\leq r,\ |g_i|\leq1\text{ for }i>r\}$, so every subgradient is $$G=\sum_k\lambda_kU_k\Sigma_kV_k^\top=U^{(1)}{V^{(1)}}^\top+\sum_k\lambda_kU_k^{(2)}W_k{V_k^{(2)}}^\top,$$ with $W_k$ diagonal with entries in $[-1,1]$. . . . 2. Each SVD satisfies $U_k^{(2)}=U^{(2)}Y_k$ and $V_k^{(2)}=V^{(2)}Z_k$, with $Y_k\in\cO(u-r)$ and $Z_k\in\cO(v-r)$. Hence $G=U^{(1)}{V^{(1)}}^\top+U^{(2)}W{V^{(2)}}^\top$ with $W=\sum_k\lambda_kY_kW_kZ_k^\top$. . . . 3. Finally, $\sigma_1(W)\leq\sum_k\lambda_k\sigma_1(W_k)\leq1$. $\square$ . . . ::: {.callout-tip title="Key Idea: sparsity comes from singularities" icon=false} A norm's subdifferential is largest where the norm is not differentiable: at sparse vectors for $\norm{\cdot}_1$, and at low-rank matrices for $\norm{\cdot}_{S_1}$. Sparsity-inducing norms are built by creating singularities at the sparsest objects. :::

  (function () {
